items.content:
일론 머스크 CEO가 미국 중간선거의 최대 패자 중 한 명으로 꼽혔다. 공화당 승리를 위해 약 5억달러(약 6700억원)를 투입했지만 민주당이 상·하원을 장악하고 핵심 사업 거점인 텍사스에서도 승리하면서, AI 데이터센터 건설과 우주사업 확장, 정부 계약 등에 차질이 생길 수 있다는 전망이 나오고 있다.

로이터와 워싱턴포스트 등 주요 외신은 4일(현지시간) 머스크 CEO가 막대한 정치자금을 투입하고도 공화당의 패배를 막지 못했으며, 그 여파가 기업 경영으로 이어질 수 있다고 보도했다. 특히 그를 이번 중간선거에서 가장 큰 손실을 본 인물 중 한 명으로 평가했다.

머스크는 공화당 후보와 정치단체에 4억달러 이상을 지원하며 최대 개인 정치 후원자로 활동했다. 그러나 민주당은 상·하원 다수당을 차지했으며, 공화당의 오랜 텃밭인 텍사스에서도 지나 히노호사가 그레그 애벗 주지사를 꺾었다. 연방 상원의원 선거에서도 민주당 제임스 탈라리코가 머스크가 지원한 켄 팩스턴을 물리쳤다.

막대한 정치자금이 오히려 역효과를 냈다는 분석도 나왔다. 와이어드가 4일 오전까지 집계한 결과, 머스크의 정치단체 '아메리카 PAC'이 지원한 후보들은 승패가 확정된 21개 선거에서 1승 20패를 기록했다. 탈라리코 당선자는 선거 과정에서 머스크가 막대한 자금으로 정치적 영향력을 확보하려 한다고 비판하며 이를 주요 선거 쟁점으로 활용했다.

무엇보다 텍사스의 패배가 뼈아프다는 평이다. 텍사스는 테슬라와 스페이스X의 본사가 있고, 머스크가 AI 데이터센터와 반도체 생산시설, 자율주행차 사업 등에 대규모 투자를 추진하는 핵심 거점이다. 이곳에서만 2억2400만달러를 공화당에 지원했지만, 주요 선거에서 모두 패했다.

이에 따라 공화당 주정부 아래에서 누려왔던 우호적인 사업 환경에도 변화가 예상된다. 와이어드는 애벗 주지사실이 관할해 온 16억달러 이상의 기업 세제 혜택을 거론하며, 정권 교체가 머스크의 사업에 영향을 줄 수 있다고 분석했다. 향후 신규 투자에 대한 세제 혜택과 인허가 정책이 어떻게 달라질지가 관건이다.

가장 직접적인 사업 위험은 AI 데이터센터 건설이다. 히노호사 당선인은 선거 과정에서 주민 보호 대책이 마련될 때까지 신규 데이터센터 건설을 중단하고 관련 세제 혜택도 폐지해야 한다고 주장했다. 데이터센터의 막대한 전력과 수자원 소비가 주민들의 공공요금 부담을 높인다는 이유다.

이는 AI 컴퓨팅 인프라를 공격적으로 증설해 온 머스크의 계획과 충돌한다. 스페이스X는 테네시주 멤피스 인근의 초대형 AI 데이터센터 '콜로서스'와 '콜로서스 II'를 중심으로 AI 사업을 확대하고 있다. 앤트로픽 등 외부 고객에게 컴퓨팅 자원을 임대하며 매출을 늘렸고, 이 사업은 상장 이후 첫 흑자를 기록하는 데도 기여했다.

스페이스X는 지난 9월 말 1.7기가와트(GW)였던 AI 컴퓨팅 설비 용량을 내년에는 13GW까지 확대한다는 목표를 제시했다. 텍사스 스타베이스에도 신규 컴퓨팅 시설을 계획하고 있어 현지 데이터센터 규제가 강화되면 건설 일정과 투자 비용에 영향받을 수 있다.

스페이스X의 우주사업에도 새로운 변수가 생겼다. 히노호사는 앞서 머스크와 애벗 주지사 사이에 오간 이메일 공개를 요구하는 소송을 제기했으며, 스페이스X의 사업 확장을 위해 해안가 주립공원 부지를 매각하는 방안에도 반대했다. 이에 따라 스타베이스의 토지 확보와 시설 확장 과정에서 주정부와 갈등이 발생할 가능성이 있다.

연방 차원에서도 민주당의 의회 장악으로 머스크 기업에 대한 조사가 강화될 전망이다. 민주당 의원들은 그동안 스페이스X의 정부 계약과 보조금, 우크라이나군의 스타링크 위성통신 이용 제한, 정부효율부(DOGE)에서 추진한 연방 공무원 감축 등을 문제 삼아 왔다. 차기 하원 감독위원장을 맡을 로버트 가르시아 의원도 공화당과 관련 인사들에게 법적 대응을 준비하라는 메시지를 내놓았다.

금융시장에서도 정치적 위험을 반영하는 움직임이 나타났다. 4일 장중 스페이스X와 테슬라 주가는 각각 한때 5.5%, 5.1% 하락하며 주요 주가지수의 상승세와 대조를 이뤘다. 결국 3.3%, 3.8% 하락으로 장을 마감하며 하루 동안 두 회사의 시가총액 약 1300억달러(약 174조원)가 증발했다.

하지만 도널드 트럼프 대통령은 여전히 행정부를 이끌고 있으며, 스페이스X의 우주 발사와 위성통신 사업은 미국의 국가안보 및 우주개발 정책과 긴밀하게 연결돼 있다. 의회의 감독 강화가 실제 계약 축소나 사업 중단으로 이어질지는 불확실하다.

머스크는 선거 결과가 나온 뒤 X에 "이제 우주 데이터센터가 꽤 매력적으로 보인다"라는 글을 게시했다. 지상 데이터센터 규제에 대한 반응으로 해석되지만, 우주 데이터센터는 냉각과 유지보수 등 해결해야 할 기술적 과제가 많다.

막대한 정치자금으로 공화당을 지원했던 그는 앞으로 민주당이 장악한 의회와 텍사스 주정부를 상대로 대규모 투자 계획을 추진해야 하는 상황을 맞았다는 평이다.

items.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
items.summary: Article URL: https://layer3intel.com/blog/residential-proxies-white-house-network Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50371246 Points: 807 # Comments: 253
items.content:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

From October 5 to November 3:

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Other remote places with activity:

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

items.title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms
items.summary: Leading the Future, backed by Silicon Valley’s biggest billionaires, had a war chest of $100 million and an aggressive stance against AI regulation. All of it didn’t add up to much on Tuesday night.
items.content:
Leading the Future, the biggest pro-AI super PAC network , is walking away from the midterm elections with just over $20 million still in the bank and a roster of dozens of successful congressional candidates from both sides of the aisle.

At first glance, that looks like a win. The details tell another story, though. The donations went overwhelmingly to safe candidates, and the results in the small handful of riskier races that Leading the Future got involved with indicate that its plans to shape the election fell flat.

When Leading the Future entered the scene in August 2025 vowing to “ oppose policies that stifle innovation ," it had a war chest of around $100 million thanks to some of Silicon Valley’s biggest tech billionaires—including Andreessen Horowitz, Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale , and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman —and was led by major political strategists.

Designed as a “ structured ecosystem ,” it set a goal of having ”maximum flexibility to engage in the 2026 election cycle and beyond.” The network is made up of 501(c)(4) organizations and federal and state super PACs catering to both sides of the aisle: American Mission largely gives to Republicans, while Think Big largely gives to Democrats. Its structure and overlapping strategists quickly drew comparisons to Fairshake, a massive, well-funded pro-crypto super PAC network that dominated in the 2024 election.

“They came out guns a-blazing, saying, ‘Be afraid, we are going to spend our millions to influence not only how lawmakers legislate us but also against you in your primaries and in your reelection,’” Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, tells WIRED. ”The purpose of that was to bully lawmakers into acquiescence, intimidate them into not sticking their necks out on AI safety or tech industry regulation at all.”

Leading the Future did not respond to requests for comment.

Late last year, Leading the Future took on Democrat Alex Bores , a former Palantir engineer and state lawmaker running in New York’s 12th congressional district on an AI safety platform, spending millions of dollars in attack ads against his primary bid.

“They fully expected to bury him, put his head on a spike, and parade it around as proof that they could,” says Haworth. Instead, Bores’ candidacy became a high-profile proxy war between competing AI philosophies, boosting his profile and platform. The pro-AI safety network Public First, which has significant financial backing from Anthropic, spent $15 million boosting Bores’ candidacy. Though Bores didn’t win, he came second in a crowded primary field to another candidate, Micah Lasher, who campaigned on tech accountability and AI safety.

Leading the Future spent about $26 million in independent expenditures on the primaries alone. But spending tapered off as it headed into the general election, as the network dropped about $10 million in total while overwhelmingly backing candidates in safe races. Its funding also dropped off , with the network reporting zero donations in the second and third quarters.

The strategy seems to have shifted around the same time that stark polling began coming back showing widespread distrust of Big Tech and cronyism in Washington, DC. (An NBC exit poll found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers played a “major” role in their vote.)

Backing safe candidates was, simply put, “an influence play,” says Haworth. ”They're trying to ingratiate themselves with incoming members of Congress.”

The co-founder of Public First Action says that the midterms marked a victory for AI safety. “Voters in both parties delivered the same verdict tonight,” says Brad Carson. “This is a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way.”

Results weren’t great in the riskier races that Leading the Future jumped into.

One of its biggest bets was on Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham and an incumbent running to serve a full term in South Carolina. Graham earned the moniker “Data Center Darline ” from her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews due to her enthusiastic support of AI and data center expansion. American Mission donated more than $2 million to Graham, who ultimately lost with 46.5 percent in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1998.

Of the other toss-up House races that Leading the Future weighed in on, almost all were in support of Republican candidates through the American Mission super PAC. The exception was Democratic Florida representative Jared Moskowitz’s reelection campaign, which it funded through Think Big. Moskowitz won by 13,000 votes against challenger Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton.

In North Carolina’s 1st congressional district, Leading the Future through American Mission backed Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel who served as an assistant secretary of defense working on cyber policy under President Donald Trump in 2025, in her primary. Guardrails Alliance, another player in the AI safety network, backed her opponent, Democrat Don Davis, who previously cosponsored a bill that would limit tax giveaways for data center development. Davis won.

Leading the Future also backed Aaron Flint, a retired combat veteran, conservative commentator, and former state director for Republican representative Ryan Zinke, who was running in Montana’s first congressional district. Flint conceded to his Democratic opponent Sam Forstag, a Democratic wildland firefighter who landed endorsements from major progressives including Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez and advocated for strict federal oversight of AI. (The Associated Press has yet to call the race.)

items.title: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system
items.summary: AT&T's smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the "first" home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your vi
items.content:
AT&T’s Connected Life system now supports Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events and more.

AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more.

With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home.

These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home.

AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs , which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

items.title: Google Is Forcing AI Overviews in Classrooms. Schools Are Searching for a Way Out
items.summary: Google is tying up AI Overviews with traditional search, angering parents and educators who worry that easy, machine-generated answers are leaving kids less capable.
items.content:
Two weeks ago, an IT administrator for an elementary-middle school took to Google’s support forums requesting a way to block students from seeing AI Overviews —the chatbot-generated answers at the top of search results.

“This seems counterproductive to what we're trying to teach,” the administrator wrote . “Students need opportunities to navigate search results, examine sources, and draw their own conclusions rather than being handed an AI-generated synthesis before they've even started.”

No one from Google responded to the concern, which has been bubbling up for years. But counterparts from three districts voiced similar frustration and pointed to workarounds they were employing or considering to block AI Overviews in lieu of an official “off” switch. Their expertise is about to be in demand.

Google announced on Tuesday that it is declining to provide schools an option to disable AI Overviews . Instead, starting next year, schools will have to block access to search altogether to get rid of the feature. The decision has stunned educators, parents, and technology researchers across the US.

“We were flabbergasted,” says Dominique Johnson, part of an Oregon community group called Lake Oswego Parents For Responsible Technology. “This move makes things even more difficult for school districts that have determined AI is harmful to foundational learning.”

Google didn’t respond to a request for comment. But in a public response to the controversy shared on X, the company contended that schools will now have “more choice, not less” because search, its Gemini chatbot, and Gemini Notebook tool will be off by default starting next year. Administrators can enable one, two, or all three services.

The issue for schools and parents, though, is that Google considers AI Overviews and a companion feature called AI Mode inseparable from the traditional search experience. Respectively launched in 2023 and last year, they bring the functionality of AI chatbots, such as Gemini or ChatGPT, directly into search results.

“Kids are already using these search-bar summaries to skip real effort, pulling instant math answers and letting AI write their essays,” Johnson says. “To make matters worse, these AI snapshots frequently make mistakes and output false facts, which younger students take as absolute truth.”

The AI-generated responses are tempting to read and often good enough to trust , triggering headaches beyond classrooms. Wikipedia , news websites, and education tools have lost human visitors as people rely on overviews. Google uses the same bots to crawl the web for its search and AI products, making it impossible for publishers to opt out of their content being used for the latter.

Google’s push to make AI Overviews a prominent part of search has already come at a cost. Last week, shares of parent company Alphabet suffered their worst single-day selloff, erasing half a trillion dollars in market value after the company reported weaker-than-expected search ad sales. A big cause? Increased usage of AI Overviews and AI Mode, which aren’t packed with many ads yet—although some experts believe the slump will only be temporary.

For schools, the dilemma over search may be just beginning. While several districts WIRED contacted didn’t respond to requests for comment, Los Angeles Unified says it is still reviewing the potential implications of Google’s announcement. Some education technology experts argue that schools should abandon Google search altogether, or at least do a better job teaching students to question the validity of AI answers.

“Under-resourced districts will grit their teeth and say, ‘we don’t have the capacity to dig in our heels and not use Google,’” says Stephen Aguilar, who coleads University of Southern California’s Center for Generative AI and Society. “A lot are likely going to accelerate plans they already have to teach students about this new digital literacy.”

Parent advocates also plan to push districts to look elsewhere. “This move just continues a well-established pattern of big tech companies pushing products into classrooms,” says Karolle Rabarison, a policy and communications strategist who helps lead Schools Beyond Screens in Washington, DC. “It’s not going to work any more.”

Tech industry veterans disagree about how difficult it would be for Google to let schools disable AI Overviews without affecting the rest of Search. “It’s a question of whether they’re committed to maintaining two versions of search in the long run,” says Nicole Kerson, a former senior Google Search product manager who runs the AI strategy firm Collected Company. “It's very hard to maintain a forked product like that.”

Microsoft offers a Google Chrome extension that lets users turn off AI-generated summaries in Bing search. Adeel Khan, a former teacher and principal who now runs MagicSchool, which provides AI chatbots for students and teachers, says it is “infuriating, insulting, and ludicrous” that Google isn’t doing something similar.

Without an official way to disable AI Overviews, schools have turned to technical workarounds, including modifying search URLs and adopting browser extensions that change how Google results appear. Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia recently developed its own extension . But these loopholes could stop functioning if Google changes how its search results are delivered.

Smaller search engines, such as the privacy-focused DuckDuckGo, see an opportunity to win business from schools frustrated with Google. “I wouldn't expect to see a Google-style ‘DuckDuckGo Classroom’ anytime soon, but ideally, we'll have special resources just for educators looking to make a switch,” says spokesperson Allison Goodman.

items.title: Knives Are Out in the White House
items.summary: From top officials like Pete Hegseth to White House aides to right-wing pundits, the race is on to find someone besides Donald Trump to blame for the Republicans’ catastrophic losses.
items.content:
President Donald Trump’s aides were reeling from the scale of Republican losses on Tuesday night, but they almost immediately began figuring out who to blame .

The ultimate responsibility, officials acknowledged only in private, lay with Trump for taking the country into an unpopular war with Iran that drove up prices, which became the number one issue for voters.

But in the absence of being able to blame Trump publicly, there has been growing pressure to find scapegoats in all places, from cabinet officials to White House aides to conservative media commentators.

Recalling how then-president George W. Bush pushed out defense secretary Donald Rumsfeld after the GOP lost both chambers in 2006, sources say there is an expectation from furious officials and donors for Trump to do something similar.

Trump does not seem to have made up his mind on whether he should, sources say, in part because of a recognition that there was perhaps not much that his staff could have done to stave off such overwhelming Democratic victories.

He has also been advised recently, sources tell Inner Loop , that it may be better to keep top staff inside the proverbial tent to ensure they remain loyal in the event they receive subpoenas from congressional investigators next year.

Still, some early scrutiny has been cast on people around Trump who have been viewed as encouraging the president to continue the Iran war even as it started to drag down polls months before the midterms.

Some scrutiny has been directed at defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the target of a whisper campaign that he kept presenting rosy military outlooks that misled Trump into believing more strikes could win the war.

The presentations had been so glowing, sources say, that a number of top officials, including vice president JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio this spring started requesting their own intelligence briefings to get a more somber assessment of the situation.

The Department of Defense did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

In other quarters, Trump advisers have been furious with conservative media commentators who they see as having encouraged the president to double down on the war even after it became mired in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz.

And still others returned to blaming White House deputy chief of staff James Blair, who temporarily left the administration to develop the GOP midterm strategy, including an effort to redraw congressional maps to favor Republicans.

In the end, that redistricting gambit backfired in epic fashion. Out of 14 key districts that got redrawn this cycle, Republicans won just one race in Texas and one race in Tennessee, while Democrats won most races in deep red Texas and Ohio by double digits.

Blair was already getting flak preemptively as polls ahead of the midterms showed Republicans down even in those races, some of which Trump carried by wide margins in the 2024 presidential election. But with many of the results now final, Blair has become a target, sources say.

Trump, for his part, spent the latter part of election night blaming the quality of candidates in key battleground races and claiming voters did not support Republicans because he was not on the ballot himself.

Still, other people in Trump’s orbit have been horrified but unsurprised that the president took no personal responsibility and denied that the devastating GOP losses were effectively a referendum on his second term.

Many of the candidates in key Senate races were people that Trump had chosen and endorsed, including the scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in Texas and the inexperienced Darline Graham, sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina.

And in North Carolina, the former RNC chair Michael Whatley was defeated resoundingly by the Democratic Roy Cooper—but only after Trump primaried the popular incumbent Thom Tillis earlier this year.

As for Trump’s claim that he wasn’t on the ballot, that was undercut by the president explicitly telling voters at rallies across the country to pretend that he was, in order to drive turnout. And at those same rallies, some advisers noted, Trump overshadowed his own message by repeatedly talking about record profits of oil companies and his vanity construction projects.

Voters, it’s clear, didn’t like that message.

items.content:
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well.

DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.

On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”

Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”

Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong. https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9

In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.

The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.

Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.

After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.

We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced: – Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control…

The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.

DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.

However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com , where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.

That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.

items.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
items.summary: “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Clément Delangue said of the need for open source AI.
items.content:
Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami.

“Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.”

Hugging Face is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught.

Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.

Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks , a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.

Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

items.title: Ted Cruz aims to stack FCC with Republicans before Democrats take Senate control
items.summary: Cruz and Trump seem to have no plans to fill FCC's empty Democratic seat.
items.content:
Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is aiming to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take over control of the Senate in January 2027.

Just before the Republicans’ midterm loss, Cruz yesterday announced a November 10 nomination hearing for Trump’s FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs. In his final two months as chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, Cruz seems set on moving the Thumann Severs nomination to a full vote of the Senate.

Confirming Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC. That could become a 3-0 advantage at the end of 2027 because FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would have to leave the commission at that time if Trump does not agree to renominate her.

Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) recently warned that federal law prohibits an all-Republican FCC and that “any action taken by a partisan FCC could be overturned in court, based on the statutory history of the Communications Act.” Wyden wrote in a September 24 letter to Gomez, “Because the Communications Act sets a quorum at three members, there is speculation that the President intends to fire you once [Thumann Severs] is confirmed, attempting to run the agency with an all-Republican 3-0 panel.”

“Under an all-Republican commission, every single license renewal, equipment certification, spectrum transfer, or other delegated action would be legally defective, casting a cloud of crippling legal uncertainty over the entire communications industry,” Wyden wrote.

Every FCC commissioner must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. By tradition, the president nominates opposing-party commissioners based on recommendations from the opposing party’s Senate leaders.

The bipartisan process has ensured that the FCC’s makeup complies with US law, but Trump hasn’t followed the tradition in his second term. He has failed to nominate a Democrat to the other empty FCC seat and has not renominated Gomez so she can continue past 2027.

Gomez today issued a statement calling on Congress to fill the empty FCC seats in a bipartisan manner.

“We must rebuild public trust in the FCC by returning the public interest standard to its original meaning as an obligation to communities rather than a tool for political pressure,” Gomez said. “That means defending the First Amendment and a free press from government interference, advancing competitive innovation that smartly protects our communications networks, and delivering real results for consumers.”

Thumann Severs is an attorney and senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Trump nominated Thumann Severs in August , but a Senate nomination hearing originally scheduled in September was postponed to accommodate her maternity leave. We asked Cruz’s office about plans for Thumann Severs’ confirmation vote and will update this article if we get a response.

The Communications Act requires the FCC to have three members for a quorum. The US law also forbids supermajorities on the FCC by specifying that “the maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

In previous administrations, the president and Senate agreed on paired nominations to ensure that the president’s party maintained a 3-2 advantage. Senate Democrats have been pushing for the Thumann Severs nomination to be paired with a new Democratic nominee so the commission can have a full slate of five members. When it became clear that wouldn’t happen, Democrats asked Trump to at least renominate Gomez in order to maintain a 3-1 split.

Twenty-one Democratic lawmakers on the House Commerce Committee wrote a letter last week to Cruz and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), urging “that any new Republican nominee to the commission be paired with the nomination of a qualified Democratic commissioner, including the renomination of Commissioner Anna M. Gomez to a full term.”

The letter continued:

The Communications Act limits how many commissioners may belong to one political party, ensuring that decisions on broadband, media ownership, and network security are tested by more than one point of view… Robust disagreement, independent judgment, and deliberation strengthen the commission’s decision-making and provide an important check when the FCC considers policies with far-reaching implications for consumers, competition, and constitutional freedoms.

Gomez can’t prevent any major regulatory actions that Carr’s majority is set on taking, but she has been a consistent voice opposing Carr’s attacks on Trump’s least favorite news organizations and attempts to police speech on broadcast TV . She also has occasionally convinced Carr to make changes to rulemakings that she argued would harm telecom consumers.

The Democrats’ letter said Gomez has been a strong advocate for telecom consumer protections, competition, network security, and access to affordable high-speed broadband. “Additionally, the FCC’s licensing and enforcement authority over broadcasters carries real constitutional limits, and Commissioner Gomez has taken that seriously, defending editorial independence and speaking out when she believed that authority was being stretched beyond its proper role,” Democrats wrote.

Gomez’s term technically expired on June 30. US law allows her to serve until the end of 2027 or until the Senate confirms a replacement, whichever comes first. Severs would not replace Gomez because Trump nominated Thumann Severs to fill a different seat in a term expiring in 2029.

items.content:
Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano.

I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers.

“Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game,” says the Xbox team . “That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive.”

Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbox Nano controller starting today. If you’re not in the US you will be able to preview a new phone controller option on smart TVs. The controller is available on the Xbox Cloud Gaming website, allowing people to use the streaming service without a dedicated Bluetooth controller.

Microsoft says “both experiences are still being tested” and that “availability and supported games or devices may be limited” during this beta phase. You’ll need to use the Xbox beta app for Android or the Xbox Accessories app on PC to set up cloud connect on the Nano controller, and the smart TV phone controller just requires a toggle of preview features from the Settings > Account section of Xbox Cloud Gaming.

items.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.ricursive.com/ripple Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50369925 Points: 252 # Comments: 90
items.content:
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding

Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.

To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.

Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).

Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.

Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today.

LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.

In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge. ¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.

Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.

Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.

Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.

Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals .

We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.

Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.

Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.

We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.

We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.

items.summary: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the r
items.content:
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

items.content:
New smartphones used to hold their value, and it was typically months before you’d see any real discounts. But with smartphone sales dwindling and budgets squeezed, some manufacturers are offering tasty discounts on their latest and greatest devices sooner than you might think. Google’s Pixel 11 range landed in August, with the slick Pixel 11 , the more powerful Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL , and the folding Pixel 11 Pro Fold , and all four phones are already majorly discounted for the first time, well before Black Friday .

You can get $200 off the Pixel 11, $300 off the 11 Pro, $350 off the 11 Pro XL, and $250 off the 11 Pro Fold. These are deep discounts on the best Pixel phones right now, and they cancel out the $100 price bump we saw across the board from phone makers this year (blamed on the memory shortage driven by AI).

The biggest savings are on the worst value, but most powerful, Pixels: the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL. Featuring classy designs, bright, colorful screens, and powerfully versatile camera systems, these are perhaps the best Android phones you can buy right now. What sets them apart from the rest of the range is the cameras, with faster lowlight performance and powerful telephoto lenses to zoom in from afar. Google’s AI features are slick and genuinely helpful, offering proactive assistance, more conversational ability, and handy photography features like Magic Capture to automatically capture photos and videos for you. Pixels are also the only major Android phones with full Qi2 support, including magnets that make for easy mounting in the right spot.

The regular Pixel 11 offers a broadly similar experience to the Pro models, with the same Tensor G6 chipset, smart features, and Qi2 25W support. But it comes in more fun colors, including the bright pink Hibiscus I tested. You can also get Pistachio (warm green), Frost (pale lavender), or Obsidian (black). This phone is the perfect size, and the sweet spot in Google’s range for most folks, at least until the cheaper A series variant comes along.

This polished update to Google’s foldable brings real improvements, and it’s impressively durable, scoring an IP68 water and dust resistance rating. While it’s not my favorite folding phone , it does have two lovely, sharp OLED displays: an 8-inch main screen and a 6.5-inch cover screen. It misses out on the better cameras in the other Pro models, but you get the same smart AI features and overall polish of a premium device. I felt it was a bit pricey on release, but on sale, it’s certainly more tempting.

CEO Carl Pei says Nothing’s first ‘AI-native’ device ‘couldn’t have been an app.’

Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen:

“Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”

Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch two pairs of AI smart glasses , including one without cameras, and an earlier rumor said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories.

Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the Humane AI pin , the Friend , and even AI stuffed animals . OpenAI is also reportedly working on an AI smart speaker with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

Apple will start checking iCloud items that are accessible to anyone who has the link for “harmful content” starting with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 updates, the company says.

“When you share an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, that content is made accessible to Apple to check for harmful content,” according to a support document reported on by 9to5Mac . Sharing something over iCloud with the “Anyone with the Link” permissions will also mean that it’s no longer end-to-end encrypted.

Apple’s support document does not define what “harmful content” is. But this new approach follows calls from protestors for Apple to crack down on child sexual abuse material stored in iCloud.

Apple says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” any harmful content that a user attempts to upload. Apple may also block or disable accounts, prevent a user from making a new account, or, “if necessary,” invoke law enforcement.

The company launched the first 27.3 developer betas yesterday , and said recently it plans to launch iOS 27.3 in December .

items.title: The Lawyer Holding Big Tech Accountable by ‘Beating the Tar Out of Them’ in Court
items.summary: Mark Lanier led the first social media addiction case to go to trial, winning a verdict against Meta and Google in March. It’s just the beginning.
items.content:
As social media giants face allegations that they fail to protect users , attorney Mark Lanier is grappling with the question: What would it actually take to hold companies accountable?

"I think it just takes beating the tar out of them," Lanier told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the WIRED World Fair on Wednesday.

Lanier was the lead attorney in the first social media addiction case to go to trial, which resulted in a verdict against Meta and Google in March. The plaintiff was awarded $6 million in damages —a symbolic victory but a rounding error in terms of the tech giants’ bottom lines.

Lanier said lawsuits in which attorneys general represent their states have the potential to orchestrate significant change, alongside greater financial repercussions. In a case that went to trial in August, attorneys general across several states—including Arkansas, where Lanier’s firm served as outside counsel—accused Meta of failing to protect young social media users.

A few days into the trial, Meta agreed to a settlement of up to $16.7 billion , to be paid out to 51 US states and territories. The social media giant also pledged to make changes on how teenagers use Instagram and Facebook , such as a default two-hour time limit. (TikTok agreed to similar limits as part of a settlement in Alabama in September .)

A $1.7 trillion-dollar company like Meta can treat such settlements and verdicts as the cost of doing business, even if the costs climb into the billions. But these cases also have more nebulous repercussions. They impact how the public— and companies’ own employees —feel about the platforms. Lanier said that, in addition to wins in court, change can come from people understanding companies’ actions and demanding accountability.

“I am not here because I'm bored on a Wednesday,” Lanier said from the WIRED World Fair stage. “I'm here because I want everybody to know what these companies do—because that type of pressure will help change everything.”

items.title: Waymo confirms it’s shaking up its Uber relationship in January 2028
items.summary: The change will set up direct competition in those markets, as Uber has many other autonomous vehicle partners on its network.
items.content:
Waymo will end its exclusivity with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets starting in January 2028, co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana told Bloomberg News in a report published Wednesday.

The robotaxi company will offer rides directly through its own smartphone app, like it does in other cities. Uber confirmed to TechCrunch Wednesday that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree. Waymo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mawakana’s comments come after reporting earlier this year by the Financial Times that Waymo was looking to get out of its deal with Uber, which was set to expire in May 2028 . Mawakana told Bloomberg that Waymo initially partnered with Uber because the ride-hail giant offered scale. But the experience for riders has been “a little bit of a crapshoot,” she said, especially because riders never know for sure if they’re going to hail a robotaxi or a human-driven car.

“It’s important for us to have that relationship with the rider. We’ve gotten that feedback from the riders in those markets,” Mawakana said.

Uber — which has many robotaxi and other autonomous vehicle partners — told Bloomberg that it was Waymo’s idea not to add an option in the ride-hail giant’s app to book a robotaxi directly.

This story has been updated with new information from Uber , and to correct that Mawakana’s comments were about the exclusivity.

items.title: Small Phones Have Vanished. Enough Phone Wants to Bring Them Back
items.summary: As flagship smartphones balloon in size, the Enough Phone offers a 5.3-inch handset. Choose between stock Android or an anti-distraction operating system.
items.content:
Do you hate the size of modern-day smartphones ? Wonder why Apple stopped manufacturing iPhone Minis ? Turned off by the unwieldy size of an unfolded iPhone Duo ? Well, then you might be interested in the Enough Phone.

It's a brand-new Android handset whose biggest draw is its small size. With a 5.3-inch screen, it's tiny in an era when most smartphone displays sit at around 6.3 inches, like the iPhone 17 .

Most smartphone manufacturers have abandoned the small phone. Apple stopped selling the iPhone Mini in 2023 because of poor sales; on the Android side, Asus was one of the few phone makers churning out compact phones under its Zenfone line , but it paused its mobile division early this year to focus on AI, robotics, and smart glasses. Sony also discontinued its compact Xperia 5 series in 2023 (and has stopped selling its phones in the US).

Smaller players have jumped in to fill the void, like Unihertz and its keyboard-equipped tiny phones. Clicks—a relatively new company that makes keyboard accessories for smartphones—is launching the Communicator in December, a 4-inch Android phone with a keyboard. Other devices focus more on digital well-being and don't offer the traditional mobile experience, resembling “dumb phones,” including the Light Phone III , Minimal Phone , or Mudita Kompakt .

But the Enough Phone, launching today on Kickstarter for $499 (with a final price estimated around $599), takes a slightly more unique approach. When you buy it, you can choose Android 17 as the operating system and access all your favorite apps on the compact screen. Or you can choose OdysseyOS from Sleke —an Android fork with a dumb-phone-like software experience.

The handsets are expected to ship in May of 2027.

Austin Boer, Brennan Jordan, and William Stults are the trio behind the Enough Phone. Boer and Jordan manage Sleke—a company founded in 2024 that sells refurbished Google Pixel smartphones running its restricted OdysseyOS, which lets users access utility apps like Uber, Google Authenticator, and Spotify, but strips away social media, games, browsers, and anything else designed to keep you glued to your screen.

Stults met Boer and Jordan years ago through Dumbwireless, which carries the Sleke Phone. Sleke's approach was entirely software-based, as it upcycles Google Pixel phones, but a smartphone with a dumbed-down operating system doesn't need much screen space. Stults also liked that, out of all the dumb phones he's tried, Sleke's OdysseyOS has the least friction—you can still access many of the apps necessary to get through the day, like Uber, Spotify, and WhatsApp. You don't have to go cold turkey .

Once the major mobile players made it clear they no longer wanted to bother with small phones, the idea for the Enough Phone was born. Boer, Jordan, and Stults have no direct experience in the smartphone or feature phone industry (though a few of Sleke's engineers do). When I asked what each of their roles is, Jordan said they haven't given each other titles yet.

The Enough Phone is a 5.3-inch Android handset with a polycarbonate build. It looks simple—it only comes in black—but you'll notice the four Torx screws on the back. Like the Fairphone , you can remove those screws and replace the phone’s battery, in compliance with upcoming European Union regulations . The phone is 12 millimeters thick to accommodate a chunky battery—around 3,500 to 4,000 mAh, as the company is still finalizing some specs—for “all-day” battery life. That’s pretty thick for a phone; the iPhone 13 Mini is a little more than half that thickness, and the iPhone 17 measures 7.8 mm.

The Enough Phone is second from the right, next to the iPhone 12 Mini. On its left are the iPhone 6 and the Google Pixel 9.

If the crowdfunding campaign hits its goal, you’ll be able to get a midrange Android phone in a size that's hard to find on the market. However, things like camera quality and battery run time are still big unknowns. If you go with Sleke's OdysseyOS, you're effectively buying a “smart” dumb phone, since you’re software-limiting your hardware so it can’t run any of the infinitely scrolling apps that demand your attention. Stults says you might be able to switch between Sleke's OS and Android in the future, but that's not confirmed.

OdysseyOS has an app store that Sleke curates. Users can manually request that an Android app be made available, but Sleke will make the final call. News apps, browsers, multimedia apps, social media, and games aren't allowed, but utility-focused apps are, like banking, smart home, two-factor authentication, and so on. For messaging, you can use Beeper , which brings all of your chat apps together in one place —so you can still respond to Instagram DMs even without the Instagram app. If you want to look something up, Sleke offers a Perplexity-powered search bar to give you text-based answers. You can scan QR codes too. Jordan thinks most customers will opt for Sleke's OdysseyOS.

“We don't want people to have this for a year and put it in the drawer or have it as a gag item,” Stults says. “We're really hoping this could be a five-year phone for people.” To that end, the company is pledging to support the device until 2032. (Most flagship Android phone makers pledge seven years of support.)

You might be wondering where exactly the demand for smaller phones is coming from if all the major smartphone makers have given up on the size. But Enough Phone isn't planning to serve the massive smartphone market—as Boer says, what his team deems successful versus Apple is very different. He points to people who still use the iPhone Mini and its cult-like following.

“They just want a slightly smaller phone, and that has yet to be served in a meaningful way since the Mini,” Jordan says. “What's not a success for Apple could be a home run for us.”

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: Article URL: https://go.dev/blog/jsonv2 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50369106 Points: 253 # Comments: 118
items.content:
Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages.

Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json :

Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream.

encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

Case-insensitive unmarshaling : When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

Inconsistent calling of methods : Due to an implementation detail, MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by encoding/json . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:

It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v) , which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types, but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions. Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.

The Compact , Indent , and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer . This limits the usability of those functions.

Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:

MarshalJSON : The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned []byte . Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.

UnmarshalJSON : The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON . Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.

Lack of streaming : Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.

Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function, then the performance becomes quadratic.

Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.

While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise .

items.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/amd-expects-to-outsell-intel-in-q4-for-the-first-time-in-history-usd17b-guidance-would-exceed-intels-projections Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50367125 Points: 509 # Comments: 185
items.content:
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.

As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.

AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.

The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft , OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.

AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.

"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.

Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.

Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.

"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."

AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.

As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.

AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.

"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."

For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.

In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.

If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.

The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

items.title: Guerrilla bike lanes: San Francisco makes illicit infrastructure permanent (2016)
items.summary: Article URL: https://99percentinvisible.org/article/guerrilla-bike-lanes-san-francisco-makes-illicit-infrastructure-permanent/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50366522 Points: 275 # Comments: 201
items.content:
When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official .

The SFMTrA , a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:

Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones , which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.

“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement , “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.

Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.

City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.

In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).

Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress .
